Real Property vs. Personal Property▾
The three layers: land, real estate, real property

Build the vocabulary first. Land is the earth's surface, everything beneath it down to the center of the earth, and the air space above it. Real estate is land plus everything permanently attached to it, whether by nature (trees, minerals) or by people (a house, a fence). Real property is real estate plus the legal bundle of rights of ownership; the rights to possess, use, exclude, encumber, and dispose. Personal property (also called chattel) is everything movable that is not permanently attached.

How things change category: annexation and severance

Property is not stuck in one category forever. Annexation (attachment) is the act of permanently attaching personal property to land so that it becomes real property; a pile of loose bricks (personal) built into a permanent garden wall (real). Severance is the reverse: detaching something from the land so that it becomes personal property; an apple growing on a tree is real property, but once picked it is personal property; a chandelier is real property until it is unscrewed and boxed to keep.

Deed vs. bill of sale
Two different documents move the two different kinds of property. A deed transfers real property (the land and whatever is permanently attached). A bill of sale transfers personal property (movable items). When a home sells, the house passes by deed; a washer, dryer, or patio set that goes with it should be listed and passed by a bill of sale.
Fixtures and the MARIA test

A fixture is personal property that has become real property through attachment. Whether an item counts as a fixture is judged by five factors, remembered as MARIA:

MMethod of attachment
AAdaptability to the property
RRelationship of the parties
IIntention of the person
AAgreement between the parties
Trade fixtures
Items a tenant attaches to run a business; display shelving, a barber's chair, a bakery's ovens; are trade fixtures and remain the tenant's personal property. The tenant may remove them before the lease ends. If left behind, they become the landlord's by accession.

Emblements are annual crops produced by a tenant farmer's labor (corn, wheat). They remain the tenant's personal property, so the tenant may return to harvest even after the lease term ends.

💡
Two anchors for this whole lesson: in MARIA, a written Agreement is the tie-breaker that beats every other factor; and deed = real property, bill of sale = personal property.
🎯
Real property (passes by deed): a chandelier, a built-in bookcase or dishwasher, a planted shrub. Personal property (passes by bill of sale): a potted plant, an area rug, a free-standing refrigerator, a window A/C unit that slides out. Annual crops are emblements; personal property of the tenant who grew them.
Physical & Economic Characteristics of Real Property▾
Why land behaves unlike anything else

Real estate has a fixed set of physical traits (what land is) and economic traits (what land is worth). There are seven in all; three physical and four economic. Learn them as the nature of land itself.

Physical characteristics — what land IS

Immobility. The geographic location of a parcel can never be moved. You can haul away soil, but the parcel stays where it is. Synonyms you may see: fixed location. Consequence: real estate law and records are local, tied to where the land sits.

Indestructibility. Land is durable and permanent; it cannot be destroyed. Improvements can burn or crumble, but the land endures. Synonyms: durability, permanence.

Non-homogeneity. No two parcels are exactly alike; at the very least, each occupies a different location. Synonyms: uniqueness, heterogeneity, nonhomogeneity. Consequence: because each parcel is unique, a wronged buyer can seek specific performance rather than settle for money.

Economic characteristics — what land is WORTH

Scarcity. The overall supply of land; especially usable, well-located land; is limited, which supports value.

Improvement (modification). Improvements to and on the land change its value and use, and one owner's improvement can raise or lower a neighbor's value.

Permanence of investment (fixity). Money and labor invested in land and buildings are fixed and long-term; the return comes slowly over many years. Synonyms: fixity of investment.

Area preference (situs). People's preference for one location over another. Situs is the economic desirability of a location and is often called the single most important economic characteristic; it is the real meaning of “location, location, location.”

CharacteristicTypePlain meaningAlso called
ImmobilityPhysicalLocation can't be movedFixed location
IndestructibilityPhysicalLand can't be destroyedDurability, permanence
Non-homogeneityPhysicalEvery parcel is uniqueUniqueness, heterogeneity
ScarcityEconomicUsable land is limitedLimited supply
ImprovementEconomicChanges value & useModification
Permanence of investmentEconomicCapital is fixed, long-termFixity
Area preferenceEconomicDesirability of locationSitus
💡
CRESS memory device; “The 3 & the 4.” Three physical traits describe land's body: it is Immovable, Indestructible, and Unique (I·I·U). Four economic traits describe its wallet: Scarcity, Improvement, Permanence, Area preference (S·I·P·A; and the A is situs).
🎯
Do not confuse these seven with DUST. DUST (Demand, Utility, Scarcity, Transferability) lists the characteristics of value and belongs to the valuation/appraisal curriculum. The seven here are the characteristics of land itself. Scarcity appears in both ideas; read whether the question asks about land's nature (these seven) or value (DUST).
Legal Descriptions▾
Why a street address is not enough

A mailing or street address can be renumbered, duplicated in another town, or simply fail to fix a boundary. To convey real property, a document needs a legal description; a precise, legally sufficient way to identify the exact parcel. Three methods do this job.

1) Metes and Bounds

This method traces the boundary by distances (metes) and directions and boundaries (bounds). It starts at a point of beginning (POB), follows each call in turn using monuments (natural or artificial markers such as an iron pin or a creek), directions, and distances, and must return to the point of beginning so the boundary closes. It is ideal for irregular parcels.

Worked example
“Beginning at the iron pin at the northeast corner of Oak Street and Main Street; thence north 100 feet; thence east 80 feet; thence south 100 feet; thence west 80 feet to the point of beginning.” If the calls did not return to the POB, the description would not close and would be defective.
2) Government (Rectangular) Survey System

This system maps land using principal meridians (north-south reference lines) and baselines (east-west reference lines). Land is divided into townships. A range is a column of townships running east or west of a meridian; a tier is a row of townships running north or south of a baseline.

UnitSizeKey relationship
Township6 miles × 6 milesContains 36 sections
Section1 mile × 1 mileContains 640 acres
Half section—320 acres
Quarter section—160 acres
Acre—43,560 square feet
3) Lot and Block (Recorded Plat)

A subdivider divides land and records a plat map that lays out numbered lots within blocks in a named subdivision. Once the plat is recorded in the public records, any parcel can be described simply by its lot number, block number, subdivision name, and recording reference. This is the common method for residential subdivisions.

Surveys

A survey is prepared by a licensed surveyor to establish or confirm the exact boundaries of a parcel, locate the improvements on it, and reveal problems such as encroachments or easements. In short, a survey shows where the lines truly fall on the ground.

💡
Three ways to describe land, remembered as M-G-L: Metes & bounds (POB → back to POB), Government survey (meridians, baselines, townships, 640-acre sections), and Lot & block (a recorded plat). A street address alone is not a legal description.
🎯
Memorize the survey math: a section = 640 acres; a township = 36 sections and is 6 miles square; a quarter-section = 160 acres; one acre = 43,560 sq ft. To size a nested description, multiply the fractions: the quarter of a quarter section = 1/16 of 640 = 40 acres.
Public & Private Land Use Controls & Encumbrances▾
Two kinds of control: public and private

Every parcel is subject to limits. Public controls come from the powers of government. Private controls come from agreements and restrictions created by owners. Knowing which is which is a frequent exam skill.

Public controls — PETE and zoning

Government keeps four powers over private land, remembered as PETE:

PPolice power
EEminent domain
TTaxation
EEscheat

Police power is the authority to regulate for public health, safety, and welfare; the source of zoning ordinances, building codes, and setbacks. It requires no compensation. Eminent domain is the power to take private property for public use, and it does require just compensation; the legal process used to take it is condemnation. When government effectively takes or ruins a parcel without formally condemning it, the owner may sue in inverse condemnation to force a purchase. Taxation funds government through real estate taxes; unpaid taxes become a tax lien. Escheat returns property to the state when an owner dies with no heirs and no will.

Zoning tools to know
A variance is permission to deviate from a zoning rule because strict enforcement would cause a hardship (for example, an oddly shaped lot). A nonconforming use is a use that was lawful before the zoning changed and is allowed to continue; often called being grandfathered. A conditional (special) use permit allows a use the zone permits only under stated conditions.
Private controls — CC&Rs, deed restrictions, HOAs

Deed restrictions and restrictive covenants; often bundled as CC&Rs (Covenants, Conditions & Restrictions); are private limits a developer or owner places in a deed or a recorded declaration (for example, a minimum home size, or no commercial use). A homeowners association (HOA) enforces the CC&Rs and collects dues. These are enforced by other owners or the HOA, not by the government. When a public rule and a private restriction both apply, the stricter of the two generally controls.

Encumbrances: easements, licenses, encroachments

An easement is a right to use another's land. An easement appurtenant benefits an adjoining parcel and runs with the land to future owners; an easement in gross benefits a person or company (a utility line). A license is mere temporary, revocable permission to use land; it is not an interest in the land and can be withdrawn at will. An encroachment is an unauthorized physical intrusion, such as a fence or roofline built across the boundary.

Public controlPrivate control
SourceGovernment power (PETE, zoning)Owner agreements (CC&Rs, deeds)
ExamplesZoning, eminent domain, taxesDeed restrictions, HOA rules
Enforced byThe governmentOther owners or the HOA
Compensation?Only for eminent domainNot applicable
💡
Public = PETE + zoning (government; only eminent domain pays compensation). Private = CC&Rs / deed restrictions / HOAs (agreements). For use rights: an easement is an interest that can run with the land; a license is revocable permission; an encroachment is an unwanted intrusion.
🎯
High-yield contrasts: eminent domain requires just compensation, police-power zoning does not. A variance = deviation for hardship; a nonconforming use = grandfathered prior use. When public zoning and private CC&Rs conflict, the stricter rule wins. A license can be revoked; an easement generally cannot.

Forms of Ownership & Co-Ownership▾
Severalty and co-ownership

Ownership in severalty means one person or legal entity holds title. With co-ownership, two or more owners hold interests in the same property.

Tenancy in common

Each tenant in common holds an undivided interest in the whole. Shares may be equal or unequal, are transferable and inheritable, and have no automatic survivorship.

Joint tenancy

Joint tenancy is associated with the right of survivorship and traditionally the four unities of time, title, interest, and possession. At death, an interest passes to surviving joint tenant(s).

Exam Scenario
Ava owns 60% and Noah 40% as tenants in common. Noah dies. His 40% passes through his estate rather than automatically to Ava.
🎯
Tenancy in common = inheritable share. Joint tenancy = survivorship.
Freehold Estates & Bundle of Rights▾
Freehold estates

Fee simple absolute is the broadest private ownership estate: inheritable, transferable, and not limited by a special condition. A fee simple defeasible can end when a condition is violated.

Determinable vs. condition subsequent

A fee simple determinable ends automatically when its stated limitation occurs. A fee simple subject to a condition subsequent does not automatically end; the grantor generally has a right of re-entry and must act.

Life estates and future interests

A life estate lasts for a named life. When it ends, a reversion returns title to the grantor or a remainder passes title to a remainderman. A life tenant should not commit waste.

Bundle of rights

Ownership includes rights to possess, use/control, exclude, encumber, and dispose, subject to law and valid restrictions.

💡
Determinable = automatic ending. Condition subsequent = right to act and recover.
Leasehold Estates & Lease Types▾
Four leasehold estates
EstateMeaning
Estate for yearsFixed beginning and ending dates.
Periodic estateRenews for successive periods until proper notice.
Estate at willNo fixed term; possession continues with the owner's consent until properly terminated.
Estate at sufferanceHoldover after lawful possession ends, without landlord consent.
Rent structures

In a gross lease, the landlord generally pays most operating expenses. In a net lease, the tenant pays rent plus specified expenses. A percentage lease includes a percentage of business sales, often with base rent. A ground lease is a long-term lease of land.

🎯
Leasehold estate describes duration/possession; lease type describes rent and expense structure.
Liens, Priority & Property Rights▾
Lien classifications

A lien secures a debt or obligation. It can be voluntary or involuntary, and specific to identified property or general against property more broadly.

Lien priority

Priority controls payment order. The general concept is first in time, first in right, often tied to recording, but statutes create exceptions. Real estate property tax liens generally have superior priority.

Air, surface & subsurface rights

Surface rights concern the land surface; subsurface rights include mineral interests; air rights concern usable space above land. These interests may sometimes be separated, sold, or leased.

Exam Scenario
An owner sells mineral rights but keeps the house and surface estate. The ownership interests have been separated.
Deeds & Transfer of Title▾
Valid deed fundamentals

A deed conveys title. It generally identifies a competent grantor and grantee, shows intent to convey, contains an adequate legal description, and is signed by the grantor. Delivery and acceptance complete the conveyance.

Common deeds
DeedProtection
General warrantyBroad warranties, including claims arising before grantor ownership.
Special warrantyWarranties generally limited to grantor's ownership period.
Bargain and saleLimited or no express warranties depending on jurisdiction.
QuitclaimWhatever interest grantor has, if any; no title warranties.
Alienation

Voluntary alienation is intentional transfer, such as by deed or will. Involuntary alienation can occur through foreclosure, condemnation, adverse possession, or applicable intestate law.

🎯
Signing alone is not enough: watch for delivery and acceptance.
Recording, Title Evidence & Title Protection▾
Notice and recording

Actual notice is direct knowledge. Constructive notice is notice the law treats a person as having, commonly through properly recorded public information. Recording helps protect interests and gives constructive notice; it is not the same as creating a valid deed.

Evidence of title

An abstract of title summarizes recorded instruments. A chain of title traces ownership transfers. Marketable title is reasonably free of serious defects or doubt. A cloud on title is a claim or defect that may impair title.

Clearing and protecting title

An attorney may issue an opinion of title. A quiet-title action resolves competing claims or certain clouds. Title insurance protects against covered financial losses from title defects; owner's and lender's policies protect their respective insured interests.

💡
Evidence finds problems. Quiet title can resolve claims. Title insurance covers specified financial risk.
Air, Surface & Subsurface Rights▾
Ownership can be divided vertically as well as horizontally.
Air rights

Air rights concern legally usable space above the surface, subject to zoning, aviation, building, easement, and other legal restrictions. Surface ownership does not create an unlimited right to use the sky above a parcel.

Surface rights

Surface rights concern possession and use of the land's surface. Those rights can be separated from mineral or other subsurface interests.

Subsurface and mineral rights

Subsurface rights concern resources beneath the surface. Mineral interests can be severed from surface ownership and transferred or reserved separately.

Severed estates

When surface and mineral interests are owned by different parties, the exam may describe a severed estate. Do not assume the person who owns the house automatically owns every mineral interest below it.

🎯
Exam method: identify which layer of ownership the facts concern—air, surface, or subsurface—then determine whether that interest was separated, reserved, transferred, or restricted.

Concept of Value & Principles▾
Market value, market price, cost and investment value

Market value is an opinion of the most probable price a property should bring under typical, competitive, arm's-length conditions when buyer and seller are knowledgeable, acting voluntarily, and the property has been adequately exposed to the market. Market price is the amount actually paid in a specific transaction. The two can be different because a sale may involve unusual motivation, special financing, family relationships, or limited exposure.

Cost is the amount required to create or acquire an improvement. Cost does not automatically equal value. Investment value is the value of a property to a particular investor based on that investor's goals, financing, risk tolerance, and expected return.

Exam distinction
A property can sell for $390,000 even if an appraiser concludes its market value is $380,000. The $390,000 is the market price; $380,000 is the appraiser's opinion of market value.
The four characteristics of value; DUST

A property tends to have value when four conditions exist: Demand; people want it and have purchasing power; Utility; it serves a useful purpose; Scarcity; supply is limited relative to demand; and Transferability; ownership rights can be transferred.

💡
DUST = Demand · Utility · Scarcity · Transferability. Do not confuse DUST with the physical/economic characteristics of real estate from Section I.
Core principles of value

Substitution: a buyer will not usually pay more for a property than the cost of an equally desirable substitute. Supply and demand: value tends to rise when demand increases while supply remains limited. Highest and best use: the use that is legally permissible, physically possible, financially feasible, and maximally productive. Conformity: value is generally supported when a property is similar to surrounding properties. Contribution: an improvement is worth what it adds to overall property value, not necessarily what it cost.

Progression describes a lower-value property benefiting from more valuable surrounding properties. Regression describes a higher-value property being pulled downward by lower-value surrounding properties. Anticipation means value is influenced by expected future benefits. Competition explains why unusually high profits attract competing supply. Change reminds you that neighborhoods, markets, regulations, and property conditions are never static.

🎯
When an exam question asks what a feature is worth, think contribution. When it asks why a buyer will not overpay compared with similar alternatives, think substitution.
Appraisal Process & Federal Oversight▾
Why an appraisal is performed

An appraisal is a professional opinion of value developed for a stated purpose and effective date. Appraisals may support lending decisions, sales, taxation disputes, estates, insurance decisions, litigation, or investment analysis. The appraiser's job is to analyze evidence and develop an independent, supportable opinion; not to "hit" a contract price.

The appraisal process

A typical appraisal assignment follows a logical sequence: identify the appraisal problem and intended use; determine the scope of work; collect and verify relevant market and property data; identify the property's highest and best use; apply the appropriate valuation approaches; reconcile the indications of value; and report the final opinion.

Reconciliation is not averaging
The appraiser does not simply average three approach results. Reconciliation weighs the reliability and relevance of the available data and methods for that specific property and assignment.
Federal oversight and appraisal independence

Federal law and regulation shape appraisal standards for many federally related real-estate transactions. The Appraisal Subcommittee (ASC) monitors the state appraisal regulatory programs and The Appraisal Foundation. The Appraisal Foundation supports appraisal standards and qualifications through its boards, including standards commonly associated with USPAP; the Uniform Standards of Professional Appraisal Practice.

For exam purposes, remember the principle of appraisal independence: lenders, agents, owners, and other interested parties should not pressure an appraiser to reach a predetermined value. The appraiser must remain impartial and follow applicable standards.

🎯
If a lender or agent tells an appraiser, "We need this to come in at $425,000," the problem is pressure on appraisal independence. An appraiser may consider legitimate new market data, but should not be coerced into a target value.
Sales Comparison Approach▾
Sales comparison approach

The sales comparison approach estimates value by comparing the subject property with recently sold comparable properties. It is especially important for owner-occupied residential property because buyers commonly compare alternatives before deciding what to pay.

The appraiser selects comparable sales, verifies the transaction data, identifies meaningful differences, and adjusts the comparables to make them more like the subject. Adjustments are made to the comparable, not to the subject.

The direction of adjustments

If a comparable is superior to the subject on a value-relevant feature, subtract from the comparable's sale price. If the comparable is inferior, add to the comparable. A useful question is: What would this comparable likely have sold for if it had the same relevant characteristics as the subject?

Example
A comparable sold for $410,000 and has a garage worth $20,000 more than the subject's parking arrangement. Because the comparable is superior, subtract $20,000. Its adjusted indication is $390,000.
Common comparison elements

Adjustments may reflect property rights conveyed, financing or sale conditions, market conditions or date of sale, location, site characteristics, size, quality, condition, age, bedroom/bath count, garages, pools, views, and other features that the market recognizes.

💡
Comparable superior? Subtract. Comparable inferior? Add. The goal is to make the comparable resemble the subject.
🎯
The sales comparison approach is driven by market evidence. Do not confuse it with the cost approach's replacement-cost calculations or the income approach's capitalization of income.
Cost Approach & Depreciation▾
Cost approach

The cost approach estimates value by considering the value of the land plus the current cost of the improvements, less accrued depreciation. A simplified relationship is: Land value + cost new − depreciation = indicated value.

This approach is often useful for newer structures and special-purpose properties when good comparable sales or income data are limited.

Reproduction cost vs. replacement cost

Reproduction cost is the cost to create an exact duplicate using the same or essentially identical materials, design, and workmanship. Replacement cost is the cost to build a structure with equivalent utility using current materials, standards, design, and construction methods.

Three categories of depreciation

Physical deterioration is loss in value from wear, age, damage, or deferred maintenance. Functional obsolescence is loss in value caused by a design or feature that no longer meets market expectations; for example, an awkward floor plan. External (economic) obsolescence is loss in value caused by influences outside the property, such as a nearby heavy industrial use or persistent external noise.

Curable vs. incurable
An item is generally curable when the expected increase in value justifies the cost to correct it. It is generally incurable when correction is impractical or costs more than the value it would add.
🎯
External obsolescence originates outside the property and is usually beyond the owner's control. A worn roof is physical deterioration; a badly outdated layout is functional obsolescence.
Income Approach, GRM & GIM▾
Income approach

The income approach estimates value from the income-producing ability of a property. It is especially relevant to investment property because investors commonly relate value to expected income and return.

NOI and capitalization rate

Net operating income (NOI) is income remaining after allowable operating expenses are deducted from effective gross income, but before debt service and income taxes. The basic direct-capitalization relationship is Value = NOI ÷ capitalization rate. Rearranged: Cap rate = NOI ÷ Value and NOI = Value × Cap rate.

Income capitalization
Value = NOI ÷ Cap Rate
Cap rates are expressed as decimals in the formula. Example: 8% = 0.08.
Gross rent multiplier and gross income multiplier

A gross rent multiplier (GRM) is commonly used with rental income, particularly residential rentals: Value = Monthly Rent × GRM when the GRM was developed from comparable market data using monthly rent. A gross income multiplier (GIM) uses gross income rather than net income and is often associated with larger income properties.

GRM is not a cap rate
GRM/GIM use gross income figures and do not directly deduct operating expenses. Direct capitalization uses NOI and a capitalization rate.
🎯
Do not subtract mortgage payments when calculating NOI for a capitalization problem. Debt service is a financing expense, not an operating expense of the real estate itself.
CMA, BPO, Assessed Value & Taxes▾
CMA, BPO and appraisal; know the difference

A Comparative Market Analysis (CMA) is commonly prepared by a real estate licensee to help a seller choose a listing price or help a buyer evaluate an offering price. It analyzes competing, active, pending, expired, and recently sold properties as appropriate to the assignment. A CMA is not automatically an appraisal.

A Broker Price Opinion (BPO) is a broker's or qualified licensee's opinion of a property's probable selling price, often requested for specific business purposes. Whether and when a licensee may perform a BPO can depend on state law and the nature of the assignment. A BPO is distinct from an appraisal performed by a licensed or certified appraiser.

ToolTypical purposePrepared by
AppraisalFormal opinion of value for an identified assignmentLicensed/certified appraiser when required
CMAAssist with listing or offering strategyReal estate licensee
BPOOpinion of probable selling price for an allowed business purposeBroker/qualified licensee subject to law
Assessed value and property-tax implications

Assessed value is the value placed on property by a taxing authority for property-tax purposes. It may differ from market value. Property tax is commonly calculated by applying the jurisdiction's tax rate to the taxable or assessed value after applicable rules and exemptions.

Exam idea
A home can have an assessed value of $310,000, a recent market-value opinion of $350,000, and an actual sale price of $357,500. These numbers measure different things and do not have to be equal.
🎯
When the question asks for an opinion of market value for lending, think appraisal. When it asks for a licensee's pricing analysis for listing strategy, think CMA.

Cognitive Weight

Application6

What This Section Must Cover

Sales contracts✓

CRESS Question Standard

Train the rule. Then train the decision.

Every section now uses two layers of questioning. Understanding questions confirm that you know the rule, term, formula, or required procedure. Rigorous exam-style questions place that rule inside a realistic fact pattern with four plausible choices so you must identify the controlling issue, not merely recognize a definition.

UNDERSTANDINGDefinitions · classifications · direct applications · formulas
RIGOROUSFact patterns · competing legal concepts · best/first/required/prohibited · close distractors
EXPLANATIONWhy the answer controls and why the tempting alternative does not
The Word for National Section IV
“Let all things be done decently and in order.”
1 Corinthians 14:40
Contracts reward order. Agency rewards clarity. Slow the fact pattern down: identify the parties, identify the promise, identify the relationship, and then apply the rule.
Contract Types & Exam Classification▾
Start with the contract's structure

A contract is a legally enforceable promise or set of promises. On the exam, classification matters because the same fact pattern can test more than one label at once. An express contract is stated in words, whether written or oral. An implied contract is inferred from conduct. A bilateral contract is promise-for-promise; each side is obligated. A unilateral contract is promise-for-performance; one party promises something if the other performs.

Do not confuse the two classification systems.

Express vs. implied asks how agreement is communicated. Bilateral vs. unilateral asks how the parties exchange promises or performance.

Case File

A seller signs a listing agreement promising to pay a broker if the broker performs under the agreement. The document is express because its terms are stated. Depending on its promises and duties, it may also be bilateral. One label does not cancel the other.

🎯
Exam trap. If the stem emphasizes conduct rather than spoken or written words, test for implied agreement. If it emphasizes “I will pay you if you perform,” test for unilateral structure.
Required Elements of a Valid Contract▾
A valid contract needs more than signatures

For exam purposes, look for voluntary agreement, legally competent parties, lawful consideration, and a legal purpose. Agreement requires an offer and an acceptance that matches the offer. If the response changes a material term, it is a counteroffer rather than an acceptance.

Competency

Competency concerns legal capacity. A fact pattern involving minority, incapacity, or another capacity issue often changes whether a contract is valid, voidable, or unenforceable.

Consideration

Consideration is something of legal value exchanged for the promise. It does not have to be equal in economic value, but there must be a bargained-for exchange.

💡
CRESS check: Agreement + Capacity + Consideration + Lawful Purpose. Then ask whether any outside rule makes the agreement voidable or unenforceable.
🎯
A contract can contain all basic elements and still face an enforceability problem, such as a Statute of Frauds issue. Validity and enforceability are related, but they are not identical questions.
Performance, Enforceability, Breach & Remedies▾
Know the status of the contract

An executory contract still has obligations left to perform. An executed contract has been fully performed. A void agreement has no legal effect. A voidable contract is valid unless the protected party chooses to avoid it. An unenforceable contract may be valid in substance but cannot be enforced in court because of a legal defense.

When performance fails

A breach occurs when a party fails to perform a contractual duty without legal excuse. Depending on the agreement and law, remedies may include termination, rescission, damages, or another contractual remedy. Compensatory damages seek to compensate for loss. Liquidated damages are an amount agreed in advance when enforceable. Punitive damages are designed to punish wrongful conduct and are not the ordinary contract measure.

Statute of Frauds

Real-estate sale contracts generally must be in writing to be enforceable. Electronic records and signatures can satisfy writing/signature requirements when applicable. “Time is of the essence” makes stated deadlines especially important.

🎯
When two answers both sound legally possible, identify what the stem is asking: contract status, enforceability, or remedy. Those are three different analyses.
Sales Contracts, Offers, Contingencies & Options▾
Offer, acceptance, rejection, counteroffer

An offer creates a power of acceptance in the offeree. Acceptance must comply with the offer's terms. A counteroffer changes the terms and generally rejects the original offer while creating a new offer. Offers can also terminate through revocation, rejection, lapse of time, or other legal events.

Earnest money, contingencies and equitable title

Earnest money is evidence of a buyer's good-faith intent; it is not what creates the contract. A contingency makes performance dependent on a stated event, such as financing, inspection, or sale of another property. After a binding sales contract, the buyer is often described as holding equitable title while the seller retains legal title until closing.

Options and installment arrangements

An option contract gives the option holder the right, but not the obligation, to act within the option period. The optionor is bound during that period if the option is supported as required. An installment or land contract involves payment over time and should be distinguished from a typical purchase-money mortgage transaction.

Analysis Pattern

Seller changes only the closing date before signing the buyer's offer. That is not “almost acceptance.” A changed material term is a counteroffer. The buyer now decides whether to accept the seller's new offer.

Agency Relationships & Types▾
Identify who is represented before answering anything else

An agency relationship exists when an agent is authorized to act for a principal. The represented party is the client/principal; an unrepresented person may be a customer. A licensee's duties depend heavily on whom the licensee represents.

Levels of authority

A universal agent has exceptionally broad authority. A general agent has continuing authority within a business or field, such as a property manager acting within a management relationship. A special agent has limited authority for a specific transaction or purpose, which is common in brokerage representation.

Actual vs. apparent authority

Actual authority comes from the principal's manifestations to the agent. Apparent authority arises when the principal's conduct causes a third party reasonably to believe the agent has authority.

🎯
Agency questions often hide the answer in one sentence identifying the client. Circle that relationship mentally before deciding which duty applies.
Creation, Ratification & Termination of Agency▾
How agency begins

Agency can arise through an express agreement and, depending on the facts, through conduct or ratification. Ratification occurs when a principal later accepts or affirms an act that was originally performed without authority. Written representation agreements are the safest evidence of the relationship and are required in many compensation contexts.

How agency ends

Agency can terminate by performance or completion of its purpose, expiration, mutual agreement, revocation or renunciation subject to contractual consequences, death or incapacity in situations recognized by law, destruction of the subject property, or operation of law.

Termination does not erase every duty.

Some obligations, especially confidentiality concerning protected client information, may continue after the agency relationship ends.

Case File

A broker acts outside authority, and the seller later knowingly accepts the benefit and affirms the act. The exam is testing ratification, not a brand-new agency theory.

Licensee Duties, Fiduciary Obligations & Liability▾
Fiduciary duty requires disciplined loyalty to the client

Core fiduciary obligations commonly tested include obedience to lawful instructions, loyalty, disclosure, confidentiality, accounting, and reasonable care. The point is not memorizing a phrase; the point is recognizing which duty a fact pattern violates.

Accounting

Client money and property must be handled carefully. Mixing entrusted funds with personal funds is commingling; unauthorized use of entrusted funds is conversion.

Reasonable care and negligence

A licensee must use the level of care and competence expected of a real-estate professional. Carelessness that causes harm can create negligence exposure.

Compensation and procuring cause

Compensation arrangements should be documented as required. A broker's entitlement to compensation may depend on the agreement and whether the broker was the procuring cause or otherwise satisfied the agreement's conditions.

🎯
Hard questions combine duties. Example: secretly using client money is not merely “poor judgment.” It directly implicates Accounting and may also create serious legal and disciplinary consequences.

Practice with competence. Protect the public. Know the professional boundary.

Real Estate Practice

CRESS Exam Blueprint10 of 80 scored items

Section V tests professional judgment, brokerage practice, fair housing, and risk control.

Current Pearson weighting: 5 Knowledge · 3 Application · 2 Analysis. Expect questions where more than one answer sounds professional, but only one stays inside the licensee's legal and ethical role.

Cognitive Weight
Knowledge5
Application3
Analysis2
Core Practice Areas
Broker responsibility✓
Brokerage agreements✓
Fair Housing✓
Risk management✓
CRESS Question Standard

Train the rule. Then train the decision.

Every section now uses two layers of questioning. Understanding questions confirm that you know the rule, term, formula, or required procedure. Rigorous exam-style questions place that rule inside a realistic fact pattern with four plausible choices so you must identify the controlling issue, not merely recognize a definition.

UNDERSTANDINGDefinitions · classifications · direct applications · formulas
RIGOROUSFact patterns · competing legal concepts · best/first/required/prohibited · close distractors
EXPLANATIONWhy the answer controls and why the tempting alternative does not
The Word for National Section V
“Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings.”
Proverbs 22:29
Professional practice is disciplined stewardship. Know your role, know your limits, serve people fairly, and do every assignment with care.
Broker Responsibility, Competence & Supervision▾
Competence comes before confidence

A real-estate professional should work only within areas in which the professional is competent or can become competent with appropriate education, supervision, and assistance. The exam may describe a licensee who is asked to handle a transaction outside the licensee's experience. The strongest answer is usually not to guess, improvise, or pretend to know. The professional should obtain competent supervision, training, or assistance and refer specialized matters to qualified professionals when appropriate.

Broker supervision

A supervising broker is responsible for establishing systems, policies, training, and oversight that support lawful practice. Supervision does not mean performing every task personally; it means exercising reasonable control over the brokerage's professional activity.

Due diligence

Due diligence means making the reasonable investigation and good-faith effort required by the circumstances. A buyer's due-diligence period can involve inspections, title review, lease review, financing investigation, and other professional review.

Case File

A new residential agent is asked to advise an investor on a complex commercial syndication. The exam is testing professional scope. The safer answer is to involve qualified supervision or an appropriate specialist rather than provide unsupported advice.

🎯
Exam pattern: “What should the licensee do first?” If the issue is outside the licensee's competence, recognize the boundary before trying to solve the technical problem.
Unauthorized Practice of Law & Professional Boundaries▾
Licensees are not attorneys

A real-estate license allows brokerage activity; it does not authorize the practice of law. A licensee should not give legal opinions, interpret a document as an attorney would, draft custom legal instruments, decide how a client should take title, or discourage a client from seeking legal counsel.

Permitted vs. prohibited activity

A licensee may generally explain factual information, complete approved forms within the licensee's authority, and point out where terms appear in a document. The licensee crosses the line when legal rights, legal consequences, custom clauses, or specialized legal advice are being created or interpreted.

💡
CRESS boundary check: Explain the transaction. Do not become the lawyer. When the question asks for a legal conclusion, the correct move is often referral to an attorney.
Case File

A buyer asks the agent which form of ownership will best protect the buyer from future creditors. That is legal advice. The agent should recommend that the buyer consult an attorney rather than select the legal structure for the buyer.

🎯
Do not confuse providing information with interpreting legal consequences. The exam often places both choices next to each other.
Seller Listings, MLS & Compensation▾
Know the major listing structures

An exclusive right-to-sell listing gives the broker the strongest commission protection because the broker is generally entitled to the agreed compensation if the property sells during the listing term, regardless of who finds the buyer, subject to the agreement's terms. An exclusive agency listing appoints one broker but may allow the owner to sell without owing the broker a commission. An open listing is nonexclusive; the broker who is the procuring cause of the sale may earn the commission. A net listing bases broker compensation on the amount received above a seller's stated net and is restricted or prohibited in some jurisdictions.

MLS

The Multiple Listing Service is a cooperative marketing system governed by its own rules. Listing brokers use it to expose property to other participating brokers. A seller's lawful instructions regarding MLS exposure must be respected.

Compensation is negotiable

Commission rates are not fixed by law or by an association. Agreements among competing brokers to set commission rates can create antitrust problems.

Comparison

Owner sells the property personally. Under an exclusive right-to-sell listing, the broker may still be entitled to compensation. Under an exclusive agency listing, the owner may avoid commission if the owner alone produced the buyer, depending on the agreement.

🎯
If the question asks who gets paid, identify the type of listing, then identify who produced the buyer, then read the compensation condition.
Buyer Representation & Property Management▾
Buyer representation

A buyer-representation agreement creates a brokerage relationship in which the broker represents the buyer. The agreement should define the relationship, services, compensation, beginning and ending dates, and other negotiated terms. The buyer's representative must protect the buyer's interests while remaining honest and fair to other parties.

Property management

A property manager commonly acts as a general agent for the owner within the scope of the management agreement. Typical responsibilities include leasing, collecting rent, handling security deposits, maintaining the property, budgeting, marketing, recordkeeping, tenant relations, and risk management.

Operating expenses

Operating expenses are recurring costs of operating the property, such as certain taxes, insurance, utilities, payroll, maintenance, and reserves. Mortgage principal/debt service, depreciation, and capital improvements are not normally treated as operating expenses when calculating NOI.

Termination and protection periods

Representation and management agreements can terminate by expiration, fulfillment, mutual agreement, revocation, operation of law, or other contract/law events. Some agreements include a negotiated protection period that may preserve commission rights after expiration if stated conditions are met.

🎯
Property-management questions often test general agency, trust-account handling, NOI operating expenses, and the management agreement.
Fair Housing, Protected Classes & Prohibited Conduct▾
Federal protected classes

Federal fair-housing law prohibits discrimination in covered housing activity based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, familial status, and disability. Separate federal civil-rights protections also prohibit race discrimination in property transactions. Exam questions may ask both the protected class and the prohibited practice.

Steering

Directing buyers or renters toward or away from areas because of a protected characteristic.

Blockbusting

Inducing owners to sell by creating fear that members of a protected group are entering the area.

Redlining

Discriminatory lending or insurance practices tied to an area and protected-class considerations.

Advertising

Housing advertising should describe the property, not express a preference for or against protected people.

Disability accommodations and modifications

A reasonable accommodation changes a rule, policy, or service when necessary for equal use and enjoyment. A reasonable modification is a physical change to the premises. The legal responsibility for cost and restoration can depend on the circumstances and law.

🎯
Real-estate licensees do not receive the same private-owner exemptions that may apply in limited situations. If a licensee participates, assume professional fair-housing obligations apply.
Antitrust, Fraud, Misrepresentation & Vicarious Liability▾
Antitrust: competition must remain independent

Real-estate professionals must not cooperate with competitors to restrain trade. Exam concepts include price fixing, market allocation, group boycotts, and illegal tying arrangements. Commission rates must be independently negotiated, not collectively set by competing brokers.

Fraud and misrepresentation

Fraud generally involves intentional deception. Misrepresentation can involve a false statement or concealment of a material fact. Puffing is opinion or sales talk rather than a measurable factual representation, but exaggerated factual claims can cross into misrepresentation.

Vicarious liability

Vicarious liability means one party may be legally responsible for another person's acts because of the relationship between them. Brokerage questions may test the broker's exposure for acts of sponsored or supervised licensees performed within the scope of their professional activity.

Case File

Two competing brokers agree that neither will charge less than 6%. The issue is not whether 6% is “reasonable.” The issue is the agreement among competitors to fix price.

🎯
When the conduct involves competitors, think antitrust. When it involves false statements to a party, think fraud/misrepresentation. When it involves responsibility for another licensee's act, think vicarious liability/supervision.
Privacy, Do Not Contact, E&O & General Liability▾
Privacy and consumer information

Brokerages handle sensitive personal information. Reasonable privacy practices include limiting access, safeguarding records, and using consumer information only for legitimate business purposes. Federal privacy requirements can apply depending on the information and business activity involved.

Do Not Call / contact restrictions

Marketing activity must comply with applicable federal and state contact restrictions. A licensee should not assume that a prior inquiry, expired relationship, or purchased lead automatically permits unlimited solicitation. The exam may test whether the brokerage has proper consent, an established business relationship, or another recognized basis for contact.

Errors & Omissions (E&O)

E&O insurance is professional-liability coverage designed to protect against certain claims arising from mistakes, errors, or negligence in professional services. It generally does not function as insurance for intentional fraud.

General Liability

General liability insurance addresses risks such as bodily injury or property damage connected with business operations or premises. It serves a different purpose from E&O.

💡
CRESS split: E&O = professional mistake. General Liability = bodily injury/property damage risk.
🎯
If the claim is “the agent gave negligent professional service,” test E&O. If the claim is “someone was injured at the office,” test general liability.

The Word for This Section
“The prudent man foreseeth the evil, and hideth himself.”
Proverbs 22:3
Notice the condition, separate fact from speculation, and identify the disclosure or expert-referral duty.
Lead, Asbestos, Radon & Mold▾
Recognize common hazards without pretending to be the environmental expert.
Lead-based paint

Federal lead-based paint rules apply to most residential housing built before 1978 and require specified disclosures and information.

Asbestos

Asbestos is a fibrous material historically used in building products; disturbing suspect material can release hazardous fibers.

Radon

Radon is a naturally occurring radioactive gas that can enter buildings from soil and rock and is not detectable by ordinary smell or sight.

Mold

Mold is fungal growth commonly associated with moisture intrusion and may require qualified assessment when material.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
Groundwater, Tanks, Brownfields & Flood Risk▾
Environmental history can follow the land long after the prior use is gone.
Underground storage tank

Buried fuel or chemical tanks can create soil and groundwater contamination risk when leaks occur.

Brownfield

A brownfield is previously used property whose reuse or redevelopment may be complicated by actual or potential contamination.

Groundwater contamination

Pollutants can migrate through subsurface water and may affect property beyond the original source parcel.

Flood zone / flood insurance

Flood-risk classification can affect lender requirements, insurance availability, disclosure, and buyer decisions.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
EPA, CERCLA, SARA & Site Assessments▾
Separate the regulator, the cleanup-liability law, and the investigation process.
EPA

The Environmental Protection Agency administers and enforces major federal environmental programs.

CERCLA / Superfund

CERCLA provides a federal framework for responding to hazardous-substance releases and can impose broad cleanup liability on defined responsible parties.

Phase I Environmental Site Assessment

A Phase I ESA generally reviews records, site history, interviews, and visual observations to identify recognized environmental concerns without beginning with invasive sampling.

Phase II Environmental Site Assessment

A Phase II investigation commonly uses targeted sampling and laboratory analysis to evaluate suspected contamination identified by prior information.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
Disclosure Duties, Wetlands & Liability▾
Turn environmental knowledge into professional action.
Material property condition disclosure

Known facts that materially affect value, desirability, or safety may create disclosure duties under applicable law.

Latent defect

A latent defect is a hidden problem not readily observable by ordinary inspection.

Wetlands protection

Wetlands can be subject to development restrictions affecting filling, dredging, construction, and permitting.

Environmental liability analysis

Environmental liability requires examining ownership history, source of contamination, statutory liability categories, due diligence, defenses, and disclosure facts.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
Clean Air, Clean Water, SARA & Environmental Impact Review▾
Do not blend every environmental law into one category.
Clean Air Act

The Clean Air Act is a federal framework addressing air pollution and air-quality regulation. Distinguish air-pollution regulation from hazardous-site cleanup liability.

Clean Water Act

The Clean Water Act addresses regulated pollutant discharges and protection of waters within its legal scope. A development or industrial fact pattern involving discharges into regulated waters should trigger this framework.

SARA

The Superfund Amendments and Reauthorization Act amended and expanded the CERCLA/Superfund framework. It belongs with federal hazardous-substance response and cleanup law.

Environmental impact statements

An environmental impact statement evaluates significant environmental effects of certain major governmental actions. It is different from a Phase I or Phase II environmental site assessment used in property due diligence.

💡
CRESS separation: Phase I/II = site due diligence. Impact statement = governmental environmental-effects review. CERCLA/SARA = hazardous-substance response and cleanup framework.

Rigorous exam-style questions place that rule inside a realistic fact pattern with four plausible choices so you must identify the controlling issue, not merely recognize a definition.

The Word for This Section
“The borrower is servant to the lender.”
Proverbs 22:7
Separate the debt, security instrument, loan program, federal disclosure, and closing step.
Notes, Security Instruments & Financing Sources▾
Separate the debt from the collateral.
Promissory note

The note is the borrower's written promise to repay the debt under stated terms.

Mortgage / deed of trust

A mortgage or deed of trust pledges real property as security for repayment of the note.

Conventional financing

A conventional mortgage is not insured or guaranteed by a federal housing-loan program.

Seller financing

Seller financing occurs when the seller provides some or all credit to the buyer instead of relying entirely on an institutional lender.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
FHA, VA, USDA, LTV & Mortgage Insurance▾
Match the program to the borrower, property, and risk structure.
FHA-insured loan

FHA is a federal mortgage-insurance program used with qualifying loans made by approved lenders.

VA-guaranteed loan

VA financing uses a federal guaranty for eligible veterans and service members under program rules.

USDA rural financing

USDA housing programs support qualifying borrowers and eligible rural properties under program rules.

Loan-to-value (LTV)

LTV compares the loan amount with the applicable property value or price base used by the lender.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
TILA, TRID, RESPA & ECOA▾
Know what each federal financing law is trying to protect.
TILA / Regulation Z

Truth in Lending and Regulation Z require standardized consumer-credit cost disclosures, including items such as APR and finance charge in covered transactions.

TRID / Loan Estimate

TRID integrates major mortgage disclosures; the Loan Estimate provides early estimated terms and closing costs in covered transactions.

RESPA

RESPA regulates covered settlement practices and prohibits certain kickbacks and unearned referral fees involving settlement services.

ECOA

The Equal Credit Opportunity Act prohibits discrimination in covered credit decisions on protected bases identified by the law.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
Closing Disclosure, Insurance & Mortgage Risk▾
Bring the financing process to settlement.
Closing Disclosure

The Closing Disclosure provides final loan terms and closing-cost information for covered mortgage transactions before consummation under TRID timing rules.

Hazard insurance

Hazard/property insurance protects against covered physical loss to the collateral and is commonly required by lenders.

PMI / MIP

PMI is associated with conventional mortgage risk when required; FHA mortgage insurance uses program-specific MIP rules.

Mortgage fraud / predatory lending

Mortgage fraud involves material deception in a loan transaction; predatory lending involves abusive or unfair lending practices.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
Mortgage Markets, Loan Clauses & Settlement Mechanics▾
Follow a mortgage from origination through the market and into settlement.
Primary mortgage market

The primary mortgage market is where borrowers obtain new loans from originators such as banks, mortgage companies, and other lenders.

Secondary mortgage market

The secondary mortgage market is where existing mortgage loans or mortgage-backed interests are bought and sold, helping replenish funds available for new lending.

Lien theory, title theory & deed of trust

Jurisdictions differ in how a mortgage affects title. In lien-theory jurisdictions, the borrower generally retains title while the lender holds a lien. Title-theory concepts allocate title differently. A deed of trust commonly involves borrower/trustor, lender/beneficiary, and trustee.

Mortgage clauses

Common clauses can address acceleration after default, due-on-sale or alienation, prepayment, insurance, taxes, and other lender protections. Read the event that activates the clause rather than choosing by name alone.

Settlement mechanics

Settlement brings together final loan documents, title/escrow functions, funds, prorations, debits and credits, required disclosures, and transfer/recording steps.

🎯
Separate the debt, security instrument, market source, federal disclosure, and closing action.

Accuracy is stewardship. Write the formula, convert percentages carefully, keep units visible, and round only as directed.
Area & Acreage▾
Formula first. Units second. Calculation third.
Square footage

Area of a rectangle = length × width.

Acre conversion

1 acre = 43,560 square feet.

Miles to feet

1 mile = 5,280 feet.

Combined area

Break an irregular shape into simple shapes, calculate each, then add or subtract.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
Value, NOI, Cap Rate & Taxes▾
Formula first. Units second. Calculation third.
NOI

NOI = effective gross income − operating expenses.

Capitalization

Value = NOI ÷ cap rate.

Equity

Equity = value − debt.

Property tax

Tax = taxable value × tax rate.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
Commission & Loan Costs▾
Formula first. Units second. Calculation third.
Commission

Commission = sale price × commission rate.

LTV

LTV = loan ÷ value.

Discount points

One point = 1% of the loan amount.

Simple interest

Interest = principal × rate × time.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
Closing, PITI & Proration▾
Formula first. Units second. Calculation third.
Down payment

Down payment = price − loan amount.

PITI

PITI = principal + interest + taxes + insurance.

Seller net

Seller net = sale price − seller debits, costs, and payoffs as given.

Proration

Use the day-count basis and closing-day rule stated in the question.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
Investment & Property Management▾
Formula first. Units second. Calculation third.
ROI

ROI = annual return ÷ investment.

Appreciation

New value = original value + appreciation increase.

Management fee

Management fee = collected rent × fee rate when the agreement says so.

Vacancy loss

Vacancy loss = potential rent × vacancy rate.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
Amortization, Buyer Costs, Debits/Credits & Advanced Closing Math▾
The hard math questions combine several steps, not just one formula.
Amortization

Amortization is the scheduled reduction of loan principal through periodic payments. An amortizing payment commonly includes interest plus a portion that reduces principal.

Prepayment penalty

A prepayment penalty is a charge that may apply when a borrower pays a covered loan early, if permitted and provided by the loan terms and law. Do not assume every mortgage has one.

Cost to buyer / debits and credits

Closing math may require combining purchase-price obligations, loan proceeds, deposits already paid, prorations, fees, and other debits or credits. A debit is a charge to the party; a credit reduces what that party owes or reflects money in that party's favor.

Transfer tax & recording fee

When a problem supplies a transfer-tax rate or recording fee, use the rate and basis stated in the problem. Do not invent a tax or fee that the question does not provide.

Investment depreciation & tax implications

Exam math can distinguish economic depreciation used in valuation from tax depreciation used for income-tax purposes. Follow the context, assumptions, and formula supplied.

Rental calculations

Property-management math can include vacancy, collected rent, management fees, operating budgets, rent per unit, and other tenancy calculations.

🎯
Math discipline: write the relationship first, convert percentages carefully, keep units visible, and follow the stated 360/365-day and closing-day convention.

Separate TREC's administrative authority from court power and private contract remedies.
TREC Structure, Rulemaking & Consumer Protection▾
Know the regulator and what authority it actually has.
Texas Real Estate Commission (TREC)

TREC administers and enforces Texas real-estate licensing law and Commission rules within statutory authority.

Commission rulemaking

TREC may adopt rules needed to administer the Real Estate License Act within authority delegated by law.

Advisory committees

Advisory bodies can provide specialized recommendations to TREC but do not replace the Commission's final statutory authority.

Consumer Protection Notice

The Consumer Protection Notice informs the public about TREC and the recovery system and must be displayed or linked as required.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
Complaints, Investigations, Hearings & Appeals▾
Follow the administrative process instead of jumping from accusation to punishment.
Complaint

A complaint is an allegation submitted for regulatory review; it is not itself proof of a violation.

Investigation

An investigation gathers records, testimony, and other evidence to determine whether a violation may have occurred.

Administrative hearing

A hearing provides a formal opportunity to contest allegations or proposed agency action under applicable procedure.

Appeal / review

An appeal seeks review of an administrative decision through the legal procedure authorized by law.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
Discipline, Unlicensed Activity & Recovery Trust Account▾
Separate regulatory discipline, criminal/civil exposure, and consumer recovery.
Disciplinary authority

TREC may impose authorized administrative sanctions for violations, including license action and administrative penalties.

Unlicensed brokerage activity

Performing regulated brokerage activity for another for compensation without a required Texas license can violate TRELA unless an exemption applies.

Recovery Trust Account

Texas provides a statutory recovery mechanism that may reimburse qualifying consumer losses after required legal steps and subject to statutory limits.

Administrative penalty

An administrative penalty is a monetary regulatory sanction imposed under statutory authority, distinct from private damages.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.

The Word for This Section

2 Timothy 2:15
Classify the activity, compensation, exemption, sponsorship, and license status before choosing.
Activities Requiring a License & Exemptions▾
Ask what the person is doing, for whom, and for compensation.
Brokerage activity for another

Texas generally requires licensure when a person performs defined brokerage acts for another in expectation of compensation, unless an exemption applies.

Owner exemption

An owner may generally sell, lease, or otherwise deal with the owner's own property without becoming a broker merely for that activity.

On-site apartment manager exemption

Texas recognizes an exemption for qualifying on-site apartment management activity under the conditions provided by law.

Court-appointed / fiduciary exemption

Certain court-appointed fiduciaries and estate representatives may act within their official authority without a real-estate license.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
Sales Agent, Broker & Business Entity▾
Texas brokerage is broker-centered.
Sales agent sponsorship

A Texas sales agent must be properly sponsored by an active Texas broker to perform brokerage activity requiring active licensure. A sales agent does not maintain concurrent active sponsorship with multiple brokers; licensed brokerage activity is performed for the sponsoring broker.

Broker compensation channel

A sponsored sales agent receives brokerage compensation through or with the sponsoring broker as required by Texas law.

Licensed business entity

A business entity conducting brokerage may itself require broker licensure and a designated broker under Texas law.

Inactive license

Inactive status means the license exists but does not authorize active brokerage requiring an active license.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
Application, Exam & Fitness▾
Passing the exam is one gate, not the entire licensing process.
Qualifying education

Texas applicants must complete the qualifying education required by current law before licensure.

Licensing examination

Applicants must pass the required licensing examination components under current Texas procedures.

Fitness / honesty review

TREC may evaluate statutory fitness, honesty, trustworthiness, and background issues when determining eligibility.

Application denial / review

An applicant denied licensure has notice and review procedures under applicable administrative law.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
Renewal, Education, Names & Sponsorship Changes▾
Keep the license current and correctly associated.
SAE / continuing education

Texas imposes specified post-licensing and continuing-education requirements depending on the license holder's stage and status.

Sponsorship change

A sales agent may move from one sponsoring broker to another through the TREC-prescribed process, subject to active-status rules.

Assumed / team / alternate names

Texas regulates broker DBAs, team names, and alternate names used in brokerage advertising.

License renewal status

Renewal filing, education completion, sponsorship, and active status are separate compliance issues.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
Texas Inspectors & Appraisers: Separate Licensing Systems▾
A sales-agent license does not make someone an inspector or appraiser.
Texas real estate inspectors

Texas real estate inspectors are separately licensed through TREC. Inspector licensing has its own levels, education, experience, examination, and standards of practice. A sales agent may recommend inspection, but the sales-agent license does not authorize the agent to perform a regulated real-estate inspection as an inspector.

Texas appraisers

Appraisers operate under a separate appraiser licensing and certification system through the Texas Appraiser Licensing and Certification Board. Brokerage market opinions and CMAs are different from a licensed or certified appraisal performed for an appraisal assignment.

🎯
If a Texas licensing question describes inspection or appraisal work, first identify whether the person is acting as a broker/sales agent, a TREC-licensed inspector, or a TALCB-regulated appraiser. Do not assume one credential authorizes all three professions.

Ask what preserves fidelity, integrity, competence, transparency, and lawful handling of money.
Professional Ethics, Competency & Discipline▾
Texas expects fidelity, integrity, and competence.
Fidelity

Fidelity requires faithful performance of duties owed to the client and careful protection of the trust placed in the license holder.

Integrity

Integrity requires prudence, honesty, and avoidance of misrepresentation by commission or omission.

Competency

Competency requires knowledge and skill appropriate to the transaction type and geographic market.

Grounds for discipline

Texas law identifies conduct that can support suspension, revocation, or other sanctions, including serious misrepresentation and improper money handling.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
IABS, Consumer Protection & Interest Disclosure▾
Texas requires specific information and conflict transparency.
Information About Brokerage Services (IABS)

IABS gives required information about brokerage relationships and minimum duties at the point required by Texas law.

First substantive dialogue

The IABS timing rule focuses on the first substantive communication concerning a specific real-estate transaction, subject to exceptions.

Consumer Protection Notice

The Consumer Protection Notice informs the public about TREC and consumer-remedy information and must be displayed or linked as required.

License-holder interest disclosure

Texas requires disclosure in specified situations when a license holder is a principal or acts for certain relatives or business interests.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
Trust Accounts, Fee Splitting & Rebates▾
Follow the money.
Commingling

Commingling is improper mixing of client or escrow money with a broker's personal or operating funds.

Conversion

Conversion is unauthorized use of money or property belonging to another.

Fee splitting

Texas restricts brokerage compensation to persons legally entitled to receive it; sponsored sales-agent compensation follows broker rules.

Rebate

A rebate is a return of part of brokerage compensation to a transaction party when permitted and properly handled.

🎯
Read the facts first, identify the governing rule, and then eliminate answers that confuse a related but different concept.
Advertising & Unauthorized Practice of Law▾
Public communications and professional boundaries.
Brokerage identification in advertising

Texas advertising must identify the responsible broker or brokerage and the license holder/team in the manner required by TREC.

Misleading advertising

Advertising may not contain material misrepresentations or create a false impression.

Unauthorized practice of law

Texas license holders may complete authorized promulgated forms but may not give legal advice or draft unauthorized legal instruments.

Owner permission for signs

A license holder should obtain the owner's required authorization before placing a sign offering property for sale, lease, or rent.

The Word for This Section
